hip:32349: Its name comes from the Ancient Greek Seirios, meaning glowing or scorching. It is the brightest star of the night sky and, at 8.6 light-years, one of the nearest to the Sun. A white dwarf companion, Sirius B, orbits it in about 50.1 years. To find it, follow the line of Orion’s belt away from Aldebaran.
hip:30438: Its name comes from the Ancient Greek Kanobos, the helmsman of a legendary fleet; it is also a city of ancient Egypt. The second brightest star of the night sky and the brightest of Carina, it is a bright giant 309 light-years away, far more luminous than Sirius. Spacecraft use it as a reference star to find their orientation.
hip:69673: Its name comes from the Ancient Greek Arktouros, guardian of the bear, because it follows the Great Bear across the sky. This orange giant, the brightest star of Boötes, lies 36.7 light-years away and has a large proper motion: it moves fast across the sky compared with most bright stars. Follow the curve of the Big Dipper’s handle and the arc leads to Arcturus.
hip:71683: Its name comes from the Arabic rijl qanṭūris, the foot of the centaur. It is the nearest star system to the Sun, 4.32 light-years away: the two main stars, A and B, look like a single star to the eye and orbit each other in 79.9 years, while Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun, lies 4.24 light-years away. It is the brighter of the two Pointers, and the line from it through Hadar points to the Southern Cross.
hip:91262: Its Arabic name, al-nasr al-wāqiʿ, means the falling or swooping eagle. Vega was the first star other than the Sun to be photographed, in 1850, and it long served as a reference for the magnitude scale. This white star, 25 light-years away, spins fast; we see it nearly pole-on, surrounded by a disk of dust. It is the brightest corner of the large triangle it forms with Deneb and Altair.
hip:24608: Its name is Latin, capella, meaning little she-goat: the goat carried by the Charioteer. It is not one star but 4: two yellow giants orbiting each other in 104 days, and a more distant pair of red dwarfs. At 42.8 light-years, it is the bright star at one corner of the pentagon of Auriga, beside a small triangle of stars, the Kids.
hip:24436: It takes its name from the Arabic rijl al-jawzāʾ, the foot of the central one, an old figure of Orion. This blue-white supergiant, one of the most luminous stars visible to the eye, is about 863 light-years away (an estimate), and fainter companions make it a multiple star. It marks one of Orion’s feet, across the belt from Betelgeuse.
hip:37279: Its name comes from the Ancient Greek for before the dog: it rises shortly before Sirius, the Dog Star. It is one of the nearest bright stars, 11.5 light-years away, and a white dwarf companion, Procyon B, orbits it in about 40.8 years. It forms a large equilateral triangle with Sirius and Betelgeuse.
hip:7588: Its name comes from the Arabic ākhir al-nahr, the end of the river: the end of Eridanus. It spins so fast that it is one of the most flattened stars known, and as a Be star it forms a disk of gas around its equator now and then. At 139 light-years, it is the bright star at the end of the long winding line of Eridanus, in a sparse area of the sky.
hip:27989: Its Arabic name, yad al-jawzāʾ, means the hand of the central one, garbled by medieval copyists. This red supergiant, one of the largest stars visible to the eye and a semi-regular variable, is about 498 light-years away (an estimate). It was the first star other than the Sun whose angular diameter was measured, in 1920, and it faded markedly in a great dimming between late 2019 and early 2020. It is the red shoulder of Orion, across the belt from Rigel.
hip:68702: Its name is Arabic, but its meaning is disputed; it may mean ground or settled land. This blue giant, a multiple star system, lies 392 light-years away. It is the fainter of the two Pointers, next to Rigil Kentaurus, and their line points to the Southern Cross.
hip:97649: It takes its name from the Arabic al-nasr al-ṭāʾir, the flying eagle. It probably rotates in about 9 hours, fast enough to be visibly flattened, and it was one of the first ordinary stars whose surface was imaged, by interferometry. At 16.7 light-years, it sits on a short line between two fainter stars, Tarazed and Alshain, and is one corner of the large triangle with Vega and Deneb.
hip:60718: Its name is a modern contraction of Alpha Crucis, probably coined from its Greek-letter designation. It is a multiple star, 322 light-years away: a small telescope splits it into two blue-white stars. It appears with the rest of the Southern Cross on the flags of several countries. It marks the foot of the Southern Cross, at the end of its long arm, and the line from Gacrux to Acrux points to the south celestial pole.
hip:21421: Its name comes from the Arabic al-dabarān, the follower: it follows the Pleiades across the sky. This orange giant, the eye of the Bull, is 66.6 light-years away; it is seen against the Hyades cluster but is much closer to us than the cluster. Close to the ecliptic, it is sometimes passed in front of by the Moon. Follow the line of Orion’s belt away from Sirius: it leads to Aldebaran, then to the Pleiades.
hip:65474: Its name is Latin, spica, the ear of grain held by the Maiden. It is a close pair of two hot blue stars orbiting each other in about 4.01 days. Its position, compared with older records, revealed the precession of the equinoxes in antiquity. At 250 light-years, it lies where the arc from the Big Dipper’s handle through Arcturus ends.
hip:80763: Its name comes from the Ancient Greek for rival of Ares (Mars): its red colour rivals that of the planet Mars. A red supergiant, one of the largest stars known, it has a hot blue companion and lies about 554 light-years away (an estimate). Near the ecliptic, it is passed close by the Moon and the planets. It is the red heart of the Scorpion, between the arc of its head and its curved tail.
hip:37826: Its name is Latin, that of one of the twin brothers of Greek myth. It is an orange giant with a giant planet, 33.8 light-years away. Slightly brighter than Castor, it is the brightest star of Gemini and marks one of the two heads of the Twins, beside Castor.
hip:113368: Its Arabic name, fam al-ḥūt, means the mouth of the fish, here the Southern Fish. This young star is surrounded by a wide ring of dust and lies 25.1 light-years away. It shines alone in a region with few bright stars: extend the side of the Great Square of Pegasus that runs from Scheat to Markab, and it leads to Fomalhaut.
hip:62434: Its name may be Latin, perhaps meaning actor, but its origin is unclear; it is also called Becrux. This blue giant, 279 light-years away, is a β Cephei variable with small pulsations. It is the bright star at one end of the cross arm of the Southern Cross.
hip:102098: It takes its name from the Arabic dhanab al-dajājah, the tail of the hen. This white supergiant, among the most luminous stars visible to the eye, has a poorly known distance: about 1,410 light-years (an estimate). It is the tail of the Swan and the top of the Northern Cross, and one corner of the large triangle with Vega and Altair.
hip:49669: Its name is Latin, little king, a translation of older names meaning royal star. It probably rotates in about 16 hours, fast enough to be strongly flattened. It lies almost on the ecliptic, so the Moon often passes in front of it. At 79.3 light-years, it is the base of the Sickle, the backwards question mark of stars that forms the Lion’s head.
hip:33579: Its name comes from the Arabic al-ʿadhārā, the virgins. This blue giant is the brightest source of extreme ultraviolet light in the sky, and a fainter companion is visible in a telescope. At 405 light-years, it is the brightest of the triangle of stars with Wezen and Aludra that marks the hindquarters of the Great Dog, near Sirius.
hip:36850: Its name is Latin, that of the mortal twin brother of Greek myth. At 50.9 light-years, it is really 6 stars in three pairs: a small telescope shows two, and a fainter red pair lies nearby. It is the fainter of the two stars that mark the heads of the Twins, beside Pollux.
hip:61084: Its name is a modern contraction of Gamma Crucis, probably coined from its Greek-letter designation. It is a red giant, 88.6 light-years away. It marks the top of the Southern Cross, and the line from it through Acrux points to the south celestial pole.
hip:85927: Its Arabic name, al-shawlāʾ, means the raised tail, here the sting of the scorpion. It is a multiple star system of hot blue stars, about 571 light-years away (an estimate). It is the sting at the end of the Scorpion’s curved tail, beside Lesath, and the two form a close pair.
hip:25336: Its name is Latin, female warrior. This hot blue giant is closer to us than the other bright stars of Orion, at 252 light-years. It marks the shoulder of Orion opposite Betelgeuse, on the same side as Mintaka.
hip:25428: It takes its name from the Arabic al-naṭḥ, the butting one, the horn of the bull. It was once shared with Auriga, where it closed the pentagon of the Charioteer. At 134 light-years, it marks the tip of the Bull’s longer horn, at one corner of the pentagon of Auriga.
hip:45238: Its name has a mixed Arabic and Latin origin and an unclear meaning, perhaps calm waters. It is a white subgiant, 113 light-years away. It is the brightest star of the Diamond Cross, an asterism of Carina.
hip:26311: Its name comes from the Arabic al-niẓām, the string of pearls. A very luminous blue supergiant, it has a poorly known distance: about 1,980 light-years (an estimate). It is the middle star of Orion’s belt.
hip:26727: Its Arabic name, al-niṭāq, means the girdle. This hot blue supergiant belongs to a multiple system about 736 light-years away (an estimate), and lies close to the Flame Nebula and the Horsehead Nebula. It is the belt star of Orion next to the Flame Nebula, at the end of the belt opposite Mintaka.
hip:109268: It takes its name from the Arabic al-nayyir, the bright one, here the bright one of the fish’s tail. This blue-white subgiant, the brightest star of the Crane, lies 101 light-years away. It sits between Fomalhaut and Peacock, next to Tiaki.
hip:39953: Regor is a name in common use, not adopted by the International Astronomical Union: coined as a joke by astronauts, it is a crew member’s name spelled backwards. This star contains the brightest Wolf-Rayet star in the sky, a very hot star losing its outer layers, and with a neighbouring star it forms a pair that binoculars split. About 1,120 light-years away (an estimate), it is the brightest star of the Sails, near the False Cross.
hip:62956: The meaning of its Arabic name is disputed; it may refer to the fat tail of a sheep. It is the brightest star of Ursa Major, a chemically peculiar star with a strong magnetic field, 82.6 light-years away. It is the first star of the Big Dipper’s handle, next to the bowl.
hip:15863: Its name comes from the Arabic mirfaq al-thurayyā, the elbow next to the Pleiades. This yellow-white supergiant lies at the heart of a loose cluster of blue stars, the Alpha Persei Cluster, about 506 light-years away (an estimate). It is the brightest star of Perseus, between Capella and the W of Cassiopeia.
hip:90185: Its name joins the Arabic qaws, bow, with the Latin australis: the southern part of the bow. It is the brightest star of Sagittarius, a giant 143 light-years away. It probably lies at the bottom corner of the spout side of the Teapot asterism.
hip:54061: Its Arabic name, ẓahr al-dubb al-akbar, means the back of the great bear. It is an orange giant with a close companion, 123 light-years away. With Merak, it forms the two Pointers of the Big Dipper’s bowl: their line leads to Polaris.
hip:34444: It takes its name from the Arabic al-wazn, weight. This very luminous yellow-white supergiant has a poorly known distance: about 1,610 light-years (an estimate). It belongs to the triangle with Adhara and Aludra that marks the hindquarters of the Great Dog.
hip:67301: Its name comes from the Arabic qāʾid bināt naʿsh, the leader of the daughters of the bier. It is a hot blue star, 104 light-years away; unlike most stars of the Big Dipper, it does not belong to the Ursa Major moving group. It marks the end of the Big Dipper’s handle.
hip:41037: Its name is modern; it was probably given for air navigation, and its meaning is unknown. It is a binary: an orange giant with a hot blue companion, about 605 light-years away (an estimate). It is one corner of the False Cross, with Aspidiske, Markeb and Alsephina.
hip:86228: Its name is Sumerian, probably from an ancient Mesopotamian star name, and its meaning is uncertain. This yellow-white bright giant lies 300 light-years away. It sits in the curve of the Scorpion’s tail, before the sting.
hip:28360: Its Arabic name, mankib dhī al-ʿinān, means the shoulder of the rein holder: the shoulder of the Charioteer. It is an eclipsing binary of two similar stars, 81.1 light-years away, and it dims slightly every 3.96 days. It is a corner of the pentagon of Auriga, next to Capella.
hip:82273: Its name is a modern contraction of Alpha Trianguli Australis, its Greek-letter designation. It is an orange bright giant, 391 light-years away. It is the brightest corner of the Southern Triangle, near the Pointers.
hip:31681: Its name is Arabic, probably meaning the brand on a camel’s neck, but the meaning is debated. This white subgiant has a close companion and lies 109 light-years away. It is the foot of the twin Pollux, on the line of stars that runs from Castor and Pollux.
hip:42913: It takes its name from the Arabic al-safīnah, the ship. It is an eclipsing system, 80.6 light-years away, whose eclipses were noticed thanks to a spacecraft’s star sensor. It is one corner of the False Cross, with Avior, Aspidiske and Markeb.
hip:100751: Its name is English and modern, the peacock, and it was probably given for air navigation. This hot blue subgiant, the brightest star of Pavo, lies 179 light-years away. It shines in isolation, probably roughly between Alnair and the Southern Triangle.
hip:11767: Its name comes from the Latin stella polaris, the pole star. It lies 0.7 degrees from the north celestial pole, so it hardly moves while the sky turns. A yellow supergiant, a Cepheid variable of small amplitude and a triple system, it is 433 light-years away. Follow the two Pointers of the Big Dipper, Merak then Dubhe; it is also the end of the Little Dipper’s handle.
hip:30324: Its name comes from the Arabic for the herald: it announces the rising of Sirius. This blue giant is a pulsating variable of the class named after its constellation, the β Canis Majoris stars, about 493 light-years away (an estimate). It lies close to Sirius, at the front foot of the Great Dog.
hip:46390: Its Arabic name, al-fard, means the solitary one: it stands alone in a region with no other bright star. This orange giant, the heart of the Water Snake, lies 180 light-years away. It is the only bright star in a wide empty region near Regulus and Procyon, and its isolation gives it away.
hip:9884: It takes its name from the Arabic raʾs al-ḥamal, the head of the ram. This orange giant with a giant planet lies 65.8 light-years away. It is the brightest of the short line of stars of Aries, between the Pleiades and the Great Square of Pegasus.
hip:50583: Its name comes from the Arabic al-jabhah, the forehead of the lion. It is a double star: two orange giants that a small telescope separates, 130 light-years away. It lies in the Sickle of Leo, the curve of stars that ends at Regulus.
hip:3419: Its Arabic name, al-ḍifdaʿ al-thānī, means the second frog; it is also called Deneb Kaitos, the whale’s tail. This orange giant, the brightest star of Cetus, lies 96.3 light-years away. Extend the side of the Great Square of Pegasus that runs from Alpheratz to Algenib, and it leads to Diphda.
hip:68933: It takes its name from the Arabic mankib qanṭūris, the shoulder of the centaur. This orange giant, one of the nearest of the bright stars of Centaurus, lies 58.8 light-years away. It probably lies roughly between Spica and Hadar, in the upper body of the Centaur.
hip:92855: Its name is Babylonian, probably from an ancient Babylonian star name, and its meaning is uncertain. It is a hot blue star, 228 light-years away, near the ecliptic: the Moon can pass in front of it. It lies in the handle of the Teapot asterism of Sagittarius.
hip:677: Its name comes from the Arabic surrat al-faras, the navel of the horse; it was once shared with Pegasus. It is a binary, 97 light-years away, whose main star is chemically peculiar, rich in mercury and manganese. It is the corner of the Great Square of Pegasus that belongs to Andromeda.
hip:5447: Its Arabic name, al-maraqq, means loins or girdle. This red giant lies 197 light-years away, and a faint galaxy, NGC 404, sits just beside it. It is the second bright star from Alpheratz, and the line from it through μ Andromedae leads to the Andromeda Galaxy.
hip:27366: It takes its name from the Arabic sayf al-jabbār, the sword, although it marks Orion’s knee. It is a blue supergiant, about 647 light-years away (an estimate). It is Orion’s other knee, across the belt from Bellatrix, near Rigel.
hip:72607: Its Arabic name has a disputed meaning; it may mean star. This orange giant, 131 light-years away, forms with Pherkad the two Guardians of the Pole. It is the brightest star of the Little Dipper’s bowl, at the end opposite Polaris.
hip:112122: Its name comes from the Māori for guardian, a name from a Polynesian tradition adopted by the International Astronomical Union. It is a red giant and a semi-regular variable, 177 light-years away. It sits next to Alnair in the Crane.
hip:14576: Its name comes from the Arabic raʾs al-ghūl, the demon’s head. It is the prototype of the eclipsing binaries: its brightness drops for a few hours every 2.87 days. At 89.9 light-years, it probably lies in Perseus, between Mirfak and the Pleiades.
hip:86032: Its Arabic name, raʾs al-ḥawwāʾ, means the head of the serpent charmer. It is a fast-rotating white giant with a companion, 48.6 light-years away. It lies near Rasalgethi, the head of Hercules; together they mark the heads of the two giants.
hip:9640: It takes its name from the Arabic al-ʿanāq al-arḍ, the caracal, a wild cat. It is a colourful double, orange and blue, in a small telescope, and has 4 stars in all, 393 light-years away. It is the third bright star of the chain of Andromeda, after Alpheratz and Mirach.
hip:57632: Its name comes from the Arabic dhanab al-asad, the tail of the lion. It is a young white star surrounded by a disk of dust, 35.9 light-years away. It is the tail of Leo and forms a large triangle with Arcturus and Spica.
hip:4427: Cih is a name in common use, not adopted by the International Astronomical Union; it comes from the Chinese cè, the whip of a legendary charioteer. This fast-spinning star, which sheds a disk of gas, is the prototype of a class of irregular variables, about 549 light-years away (an estimate). It is the middle star of the W of Cassiopeia.
hip:61932: Muhlifain is a name in common use, not adopted by the International Astronomical Union; it is Arabic, but its meaning is disputed and may be oath. It is a close binary of two similar white stars, 130 light-years away. It probably lies in the body of the Centaur, near the Southern Cross.
hip:39429: Its name comes from the Ancient Greek for ship. It is one of the hottest and most massive stars visible to the eye, about 1,080 light-years away (an estimate), and a runaway star, moving fast through space. It probably lies between Sirius and the False Cross, and it is the brightest star of Puppis.
hip:45556: Its name comes from the Ancient Greek for little shield, an ornament of a ship’s stern. It is a white supergiant, about 766 light-years away (an estimate). It is one corner of the False Cross, with Avior, Markeb and Alsephina.
hip:44816: Its name is Arabic: it was given to several bright stars, and it is also the Arabic name of Canopus. It is an orange supergiant and an irregular variable, about 545 light-years away (an estimate). It probably lies in the Sails, near the False Cross.
hip:65378: Its Arabic name, al-miʾzar, means the girdle. It forms a naked-eye pair with Alcor, and a small telescope splits Mizar itself; it was the first spectroscopic binary discovered, in 1889. At 85.8 light-years, it is the middle star of the Big Dipper’s handle, with Alcor beside it.
hip:76267: It takes its name from the Arabic nayyir al-fakkah, the bright one of the broken ring; it is also called Gemma, the jewel. It is an eclipsing binary that probably dims slightly every 17.36 days, 75 light-years away. It is the jewel of the semicircle of the Northern Crown, between Arcturus and Vega.
hip:100453: Its name comes from the Arabic ṣadr al-dajājah, the breast of the hen. This yellow-white supergiant is surrounded by a faint nebula, IC 1318, about 1,830 light-years away (an estimate). It is the centre of the Northern Cross, where the long and short arms meet.
hip:3179: Its Arabic name, ṣadr, means the breast of the seated queen. It is an orange giant, 228 light-years away. It is the second star of the W of Cassiopeia, between Caph and the middle star.
hip:87833: It takes its name from the Arabic raʾs al-tinnīn, the head of the dragon. Observing it led to the discovery of the aberration of starlight in the 18th century. This orange giant, 154 light-years away, is the brightest of the four stars of the Dragon’s head, near Vega.
hip:25930: Its name comes from the Arabic al-minṭaqah, the belt. It lies 0.3 degrees from the celestial equator, and it is a multiple, partly eclipsing system about 692 light-years away (an estimate). It is the belt star of Orion next to Bellatrix, at the end opposite Alnitak.
hip:746: Its Arabic name, al-kaff al-khaḍīb, means the stained hand. It is a pulsating variable of the δ Scuti class, 54.7 light-years away. It probably lies at the end of the W of Cassiopeia nearest to the Great Square of Pegasus.
hip:66657: Birdun is a name in common use, not adopted by the International Astronomical Union; its origin is unverified. It is a blue giant and a β Cephei pulsating variable, 427 light-years away. It probably lies in the body of the Centaur, near Hadar.
hip:78401: It takes its name from the Arabic al-jabhah, the forehead of the scorpion. It is a Be star that brightened markedly from 2000, about 491 light-years away (an estimate). It is the middle and brightest star of the arc that forms the Scorpion’s head, near Antares.
hip:82396: Its name comes from Wardaman, an Aboriginal Australian language; it was adopted by the International Astronomical Union, and its meaning is uncertain. It is an orange giant, 63.7 light-years away. It is probably the first bright star of the Scorpion’s tail beyond Antares.
hip:71860: Men is a name in common use, not adopted by the International Astronomical Union; its origin is unverified. It is a blue giant and a β Cephei pulsating variable, the brightest star of Lupus, 465 light-years away. It probably lies between the Centaur and the Scorpion.
hip:53910: Its name comes from the Arabic al-maraqq, the loins of the bear. It is a white star, probably with a disk of dust, 79.7 light-years away. With Dubhe, it forms the two Pointers of the Big Dipper’s bowl: their line leads to Polaris.
hip:71352: This star has no proper name; it is known by its Greek letter, η Centauri. It is a fast-spinning blue star that sheds a disk of gas (a Be star), 306 light-years away. It probably lies in the Centaur, near its border with Lupus.
hip:72105: Its Arabic name, al-izār, means veil or girdle; it is also called Pulcherrima, the most beautiful. It is a colourful double, orange and blue, that needs a good small telescope, 203 light-years away. It sits in the kite of Boötes, near Arcturus.
hip:86670: Girtab is a name in common use, not adopted by the International Astronomical Union; it is the ancient Mesopotamian, Sumerian, name of the scorpion. It is a blue giant and a β Cephei pulsating variable, 483 light-years away. It lies in the curve of the Scorpion’s tail, near the sting.
hip:107315: It takes its name from the Arabic anf al-faras, the horse’s nose. It is an orange supergiant, about 690 light-years away (an estimate). It is the nose of Pegasus, away from the Great Square; the globular cluster M15 lies close by.
hip:2081: Its name comes from the Arabic al-ʿanqāʾ, the phoenix; it is a modern name. It is an orange giant with a companion, 84.7 light-years away. It is the brightest star of the Phoenix, between Achernar and Fomalhaut.
hip:58001: Its Arabic name, fakhidh al-dubb, means the thigh of the bear. It belongs to the Ursa Major moving group, like most stars of the Big Dipper, and lies 83.2 light-years away. It is the corner of the Big Dipper’s bowl diagonally opposite Dubhe.
hip:84012: It takes its name from the Arabic for the preceding one. It is a binary of two white stars, 88.4 light-years away. It probably lies in the lower body of Ophiuchus, near the Scorpion.
hip:35904: Its name comes from the Arabic al-ʿudhrah, the virginity. It is a blue supergiant whose distance is poorly known: about 1,990 light-years (an estimate). It is the tail of the Great Dog, at the end of the triangle with Wezen and Adhara.
hip:105199: Its Arabic name, al-dhirāʿ al-yamīn, means the right arm. It spins fast and is flattened, 49 light-years away; because of precession, it will be one of the future pole stars. It is the brightest corner of the house shape of Cepheus, near the W of Cassiopeia.
hip:113881: Its name probably comes from the Arabic sāq, the shin. It is a red giant and a semi-regular variable, 196 light-years away. It is the corner of the Great Square of Pegasus between Alpheratz and Markab.
hip:45941: It takes its name from the Arabic markab, vehicle or ship. It is a hot blue subgiant with a close companion, about 572 light-years away (an estimate). It is one corner of the False Cross, with Avior, Aspidiske and Alsephina.
hip:102488: Its name comes from the Arabic janāḥ, the wing, here that of the hen. It is an orange giant, 72.7 light-years away. It is one end of the cross arm of the Northern Cross, the Swan’s wing.
hip:113963: Its Arabic name, markab al-faras, means the horse’s saddle. It is a blue-white giant, 133 light-years away. It is the corner of the Great Square of Pegasus diagonally opposite Alpheratz.
And: Andromeda is among the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century. It shows the princess chained to a rock as an offering to a sea monster, then rescued by Perseus. A chain of stars starts at Alpheratz, the corner of the Great Square of Pegasus; the constellation holds the Andromeda Galaxy, the nearest large spiral galaxy, visible to the eye, and a planetary nebula, the Blue Snowball.
Ant: This is one of the 14 constellations created in the 18th century by a French astronomer after observing from the Cape of Good Hope; most are named after instruments of science and the arts. It shows the air pump, a recent invention of physics at the time. It is a faint area between the long body of Hydra and the Sails of Vela, with the spiral galaxy NGC 2997, seen face-on.
Aps: This is one of the 12 constellations formed in the late 16th century from the observations of Dutch navigators in the southern seas. It shows the bird of paradise, a bird of New Guinea then known in Europe only from skins. It is a faint group close to the south celestial pole, next to the Southern Triangle, and it holds the globular cluster NGC 6101.
Aql: Aquila is one of the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the eagle that carried the thunderbolts of Zeus. Altair, flanked by two fainter stars, marks it, and it is the brightest star of the constellation, at magnitude 0.76. Aquila lies on the Milky Way and holds the open cluster NGC 6709 and the planetary nebula NGC 6751.
Aqr: Aquarius belongs to the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the water bearer pouring water from a jar, often the cupbearer of the gods in Greek myth. It is a wide, faint zodiac constellation between Pegasus and Fomalhaut, with a small Y-shaped group of stars, the Water Jar. It holds the Helix Nebula, one of the nearest planetary nebulae, and the bright globular cluster M2.
Ara: Ara is among the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the altar on which the gods swore an alliance before their war against the Titans. It lies next to the curved tail of the Scorpion, toward the Southern Triangle. It holds NGC 6397, one of the nearest globular clusters, and NGC 6193, an open cluster with a nebula.
Ari: Aries is one of the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the ram with the golden fleece of Greek myth. It is a short line of stars, Hamal at its end, between the Pleiades and the Great Square of Pegasus. Hamal, at magnitude 2, is its brightest star, and the spiral galaxy NGC 772 lies in it.
Aur: Auriga belongs to the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: a charioteer, shown carrying a goat and her kids. A large pentagon of stars with Capella at one corner stands beside the horns of Taurus, and Capella, at magnitude 0.08, is its brightest star. Three open clusters lie in it: M36, M37 (a rich one) and M38.
Boo: Boötes is among the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the herdsman who drives the Great Bear around the pole. It is a kite of stars with Arcturus at its base, and the arc of the Big Dipper’s handle leads to it. It holds NGC 5466, a loose globular cluster.
CMa: Canis Major is one of the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the great dog, one of the hunting dogs of Orion. Sirius, its brightest star, marks it: follow Orion’s belt away from Aldebaran. The open cluster M41 is visible to the eye, and NGC 2362 is a young open cluster around a bright star.
CMi: Canis Minor belongs to the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the small dog, the second hunting dog of Orion. It has only Procyon, its brightest star, at magnitude 0.4, and one fainter star, Gomeisa. Procyon forms a large triangle with Sirius and Betelgeuse.
CVn: This is one of the 7 constellations created by a Polish astronomer at the end of the 17th century that are still in use, to fill gaps between older figures. It shows the two hunting dogs held by the Herdsman. A pair of stars next to the Big Dipper’s handle, made of its brightest star and a neighbour, marks it; it holds the Whirlpool Galaxy, a spiral with a companion, the globular cluster M3 and the spiral galaxy M94, with its bright core.
Cae: A French astronomer created this constellation in the 18th century after observing from the Cape of Good Hope; it is one of 14 figures, most of them named after instruments of science and the arts. It shows the engraver’s chisel. It is a small faint group between Eridanus and Columba.
Cam: Camelopardalis is a modern constellation, introduced at the beginning of the 17th century by a Flemish-Dutch mapmaker; the giraffe was then called a camel-leopard. It is a large faint area between Capella, Cassiopeia and the pole star. It holds the spiral galaxy NGC 2403 and IC 342, a large face-on spiral galaxy, dimmed by the dust of the Milky Way.
Cap: Capricornus is among the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the sea goat, a creature half goat and half fish. It is a large triangle of faint stars, along the line from Vega through Altair. Deneb Algedi is its brightest star, and the globular cluster M30 lies in it.
Car: Carina is the keel of the ship Argo of the Argonauts: part of a constellation of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century that was split into three in the 18th century. Canopus marks one end; the other holds the Diamond Cross and the bright Carina Nebula on the Milky Way. It also holds IC 2602, an open cluster visible to the eye nicknamed the Southern Pleiades, and NGC 3532, a rich open cluster.
Cas: Cassiopeia is one of the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the vain queen of Ethiopia, mother of Andromeda, seated on her throne. A W of five stars on the Milky Way marks it, across the pole star from the Big Dipper. It holds the open clusters M52, M103 and NGC 457.
Cen: Centaurus belongs to the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: a centaur, half man and half horse, often identified with a wise centaur. The two Pointers, Rigil Kentaurus and Hadar, mark its feet, next to the Southern Cross. It holds Omega Centauri, the largest and brightest globular cluster of the Milky Way, and Centaurus A, a giant galaxy crossed by a band of dust.
Cep: Cepheus is among the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the king of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda. Its house-shaped figure lies between the W of Cassiopeia and the pole star, and Alderamin is its brightest corner. It holds the Iris Nebula, a reflection nebula, and IC 1396, a large nebula with a dark trunk of dust.
Cet: Cetus is one of the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the sea monster sent to devour Andromeda. It is a large area next to Pisces and Aries; the side of the Great Square of Pegasus from Alpheratz to Algenib leads to Diphda, probably its brightest star. It holds M77, a bright spiral galaxy with an active nucleus, and the planetary nebula NGC 246.
Cha: It belongs to the 12 constellations formed in the late 16th century from the observations of Dutch navigators in the southern seas. It shows the chameleon. It is a small faint group close to the south celestial pole, and it holds the planetary nebula NGC 3195.
Cir: It belongs to the 14 constellations created in the 18th century by a French astronomer after his observations from the Cape of Good Hope, most of them named after instruments of science and the arts. It shows the pair of compasses used by draughtsmen. It is a small group next to Rigil Kentaurus, between that star and the Southern Triangle.
Cnc: Cancer belongs to the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the crab sent to hinder Heracles in his fight against the Hydra. It is the faintest zodiac constellation, between Gemini and Leo, and its Beehive cluster is a hazy patch in the middle. That open cluster, M44 (Praesepe), is visible to the eye; M67 is one of the oldest known open clusters.
Col: Columba is a modern constellation, drawn by a Flemish-Dutch mapmaker at the end of the 16th century: the dove sent out from the ark to find land. It probably lies next to Lepus, along the line from Orion toward Canopus. It holds the globular cluster NGC 1851.
Com: An asterism named in antiquity, this constellation probably became a figure in its own right in the 16th century. It shows the hair of a queen of ancient Egypt, offered to the gods for her husband’s safe return and placed among the stars. A loose cluster of faint stars, visible to the eye, between Denebola and Arcturus marks it. It holds the Black Eye Galaxy (M64), the globular cluster M53 and the Needle Galaxy (NGC 4565), a spiral seen edge-on.
CrA: Corona Australis is among the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: a crown or wreath, lying at the feet of the Archer. A small arc of faint stars next to the Teapot of Sagittarius marks it. It holds the globular cluster NGC 6541.
CrB: Corona Borealis is one of the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the crown given to Ariadne at her wedding with Dionysus. It is a small semicircle of stars, Alphecca at its centre, between Arcturus and Vega, and Alphecca, at magnitude 2.22, is its brightest. T Coronae Borealis is a recurrent nova that flares up after long intervals.
Crt: Crater belongs to the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the cup of Apollo, carried by the Crow. It is a faint cup shape on the back of Hydra, beside the Crow.
Cru: The Southern Cross shows a cross and is the smallest of the 88 constellations, at 68 square degrees. Its stars belonged to the Centaur in antiquity; navigators and mapmakers probably made it a separate figure in the 16th century. A compact cross of four bright stars on the Milky Way, next to the two Pointers, marks it: do not confuse it with the larger False Cross. It holds the Jewel Box (NGC 4755), a colourful open cluster, and the Coalsack, a dark nebula visible to the eye against the Milky Way.
Crv: Corvus is among the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the crow sent by Apollo to fetch water, punished for its lie. A small quadrilateral of stars next to Spica marks it. It holds the Antennae (NGC 4038 and NGC 4039), a pair of colliding galaxies, and the planetary nebula NGC 4361.
Cyg: Cygnus is one of the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the swan, a form taken by Zeus in several myths. The Northern Cross stretches along the Milky Way, Deneb at its top, and Deneb forms a large triangle with Vega and Altair. It holds the North America Nebula (NGC 7000), part of the Veil Nebula (NGC 6960), a supernova remnant, and the open cluster M39.
Del: Delphinus belongs to the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the dolphin that persuaded a sea nymph to marry Poseidon, or that saved a musician from drowning. A small diamond of stars with a tail, next to Altair, marks it. It holds the globular cluster NGC 6934.
Dor: A constellation formed in the late 16th century, it is one of the 12 drawn from the observations of Dutch navigators in the southern seas. It shows the dolphinfish (dorado), later sometimes drawn as a swordfish. Look for the Large Cloud, a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way and a pale patch visible to the eye: Dorado holds most of it, with the Tarantula Nebula, NGC 2070.
Dra: Draco is among the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the dragon that guarded the golden apples of the Hesperides. It is a long winding line between the two Dippers, its head a quadrilateral of stars near Vega. Eltanin, at magnitude 2.23, is its brightest star, and the Cat’s Eye Nebula (NGC 6543) is a planetary nebula.
Equ: Equuleus is one of the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the foal, a small horse next to Pegasus. It is a tiny faint group between Delphinus and the nose of Pegasus.
Eri: Eridanus belongs to the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: a river, identified with the Po or the Nile, into which Phaethon fell. A long winding line of stars runs from near Rigel to Achernar, its brightest star, at magnitude 0.45. It holds the barred spiral galaxy NGC 1300 and the planetary nebula NGC 1535.
For: This is one of the 14 constellations created in the 18th century by a French astronomer after observing from the Cape of Good Hope; most are named after instruments of science and the arts. It shows the chemical furnace. It is a faint area enclosed by the loop of Eridanus, next to Cetus, with the large barred spiral galaxy NGC 1365 and NGC 1316, a radio galaxy.
Gem: Gemini is among the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: Castor and Pollux, the inseparable brothers of Greek myth. Two parallel lines of stars, headed by Castor and Pollux, lie beside Orion and Procyon. Pollux, at magnitude 1.16, is the brightest; the open cluster M35 is visible to the eye, and NGC 2392 is the Clown Face Nebula, a planetary nebula.
Gru: This is one of the 12 constellations formed in the late 16th century from the observations of Dutch navigators in the southern seas. It shows the crane, the bird. A long line of stars with Alnair and Tiaki marks it, next to Fomalhaut, and Alnair, at magnitude 1.73, is its brightest star.
Her: Hercules is one of the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the hero Heracles, often shown kneeling, his foot on the dragon’s head. A quadrilateral of stars, the Keystone, lies between Vega and Arcturus; M13, the Great Hercules Cluster, a bright globular cluster, sits on one of its sides. M92 is another globular cluster.
Hor: A French astronomer created this constellation in the 18th century after observing from the Cape of Good Hope; it is one of 14 figures, most of them named after instruments of science and the arts. It shows the pendulum clock. It is a faint line of stars next to Achernar, with the globular cluster NGC 1261.
Hya: Hydra belongs to the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the many-headed water snake killed by Heracles. It is the largest of the 88 constellations, at 1,303 square degrees. A long chain of stars runs from a small head between Procyon and Regulus to the region near Libra; Alphard, isolated, is its heart. It holds the barred spiral galaxy M83, the open cluster M48 and the planetary nebula Ghost of Jupiter (NGC 3242).
Hyi: It belongs to the 12 constellations formed in the late 16th century from the observations of Dutch navigators in the southern seas. It shows the small water snake. It is a large faint triangle between Achernar and the two satellite galaxies of the Milky Way, the Clouds.
Ind: A constellation formed in the late 16th century, it is one of the 12 drawn from the observations of Dutch navigators in the southern seas. It shows an Indian, in the sense of a native of the lands visited by the navigators. It is a faint area between the Crane and the Peacock.
LMi: It belongs to the 7 constellations that a Polish astronomer created at the end of the 17th century to fill gaps between older figures; all are still in use. It shows the small lion. It has only a few faint stars, between the Sickle of Leo and the bowl of the Big Dipper.
Lac: A modern constellation, created by a Polish astronomer at the end of the 17th century to fill gaps between older figures: it is one of the 7 still in use. It shows the lizard. It is a small zigzag of faint stars between Cygnus and the W of Cassiopeia, with the open cluster NGC 7243 and BL Lacertae, the prototype of a class of active galaxies.
Leo: Leo is among the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the lion of Nemea, killed by Heracles in the first of his labours. The Sickle, a backwards question mark ending in Regulus, and a triangle ending in Denebola draw it. Regulus, at magnitude 1.36, is its brightest star; M65, M66 and NGC 3628, an edge-on spiral, form the Leo Triplet.
Lep: Lepus is one of the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the hare, hunted by Orion and his dogs. It is a small group of stars at the feet of Orion, next to Rigel. It holds the globular cluster M79.
Lib: Libra belongs to the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the scales, whose stars were once the claws of the Scorpion. It is a quadrilateral of faint stars between Spica and Antares. Zubeneschamali is its brightest star, and the loose globular cluster NGC 5897 lies in it.
Lup: Lupus is among the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the wild animal speared by the Centaur, later seen as a wolf. It lies between the Centaur and the Scorpion, next to Rigil Kentaurus and Hadar. Its brightest star has a magnitude of 2.3, and it holds the globular cluster NGC 5986 and NGC 5822, a large open cluster.
Lyn: This is one of the 7 constellations created by a Polish astronomer at the end of the 17th century that are still in use, to fill gaps between older figures. It shows the lynx; it was said one needed the eyes of a lynx to see it. It is a long faint line of stars between Capella and the bowl of the Big Dipper, with NGC 2419, a remote globular cluster.
Lyr: Lyra is one of the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the lyre of Orpheus, the musician of Greek myth. Vega and a small parallelogram of stars mark it; Vega forms a large triangle with Deneb and Altair, and at magnitude 0.03 it is the brightest star of the constellation. It holds M57, the Ring Nebula, a planetary nebula, and the globular cluster M56.
Men: It belongs to the 14 constellations created in the 18th century by a French astronomer after his observations from the Cape of Good Hope, most of them named after instruments of science and the arts. It shows Table Mountain, the flat-topped mountain above Cape Town. It is a very faint area next to the Large Cloud, near the south celestial pole, and it holds part of that galaxy.
Mic: This is one of the 14 constellations created in the 18th century by a French astronomer after observing from the Cape of Good Hope; most are named after instruments of science and the arts. It shows the microscope. It is probably a faint area between Sagittarius and Fomalhaut.
Mon: Monoceros is a modern constellation, introduced at the beginning of the 17th century by a Flemish-Dutch mapmaker. It shows the unicorn. It is a faint area inside the large triangle formed by Sirius, Procyon and Betelgeuse, with NGC 2244, the cluster at the centre of the Rosette Nebula, NGC 2264, the Christmas Tree Cluster and Cone Nebula, and the open cluster M50.
Mus: This is one of the 12 constellations formed in the late 16th century from the observations of Dutch navigators in the southern seas. It shows the fly. It is a small group just next to the Southern Cross, near the Coalsack, with the globular clusters NGC 4833 and NGC 4372.
Nor: A French astronomer created this constellation in the 18th century after observing from the Cape of Good Hope; it is one of 14 figures, most of them named after instruments of science and the arts. It shows the carpenter’s square. It is a faint area on the Milky Way between the Southern Triangle and the Scorpion, with the open cluster NGC 6087.
Oct: It belongs to the 14 constellations created in the 18th century by a French astronomer after his observations from the Cape of Good Hope, most of them named after instruments of science and the arts. It shows the octant, an instrument of navigation; it holds the south celestial pole. It is a faint area around that pole, toward which the long axis of the Southern Cross points.
Oph: Ophiuchus belongs to the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the serpent bearer, the healer Asclepius holding a serpent. It is a large house-shaped figure next to the Scorpion’s head, with Rasalhague probably at its tip near Hercules; Rasalhague, at magnitude 2.08, is its brightest star. It holds the globular clusters M10 and M12 and the open cluster IC 4665.
Ori: Orion is among the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the giant hunter of Greek myth. Three stars in a short straight line, the belt, framed by Betelgeuse and Rigel, mark it; Rigel, at magnitude 0.18, is its brightest star. The Orion Nebula is visible to the eye in the sword hanging from the belt; the constellation also holds M78, a reflection nebula, and the Flame Nebula, next to Alnitak.
Pav: It belongs to the 12 constellations formed in the late 16th century from the observations of Dutch navigators in the southern seas. It shows the peacock. Peacock, a lone bright star, marks it, probably between the Crane and the Southern Triangle; NGC 6752 is a bright globular cluster and NGC 6744 a large spiral galaxy.
Peg: Pegasus is one of the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the winged horse born from the blood of Medusa. The Great Square, four stars of similar brightness with one corner, Alpheratz, belonging to Andromeda, marks it. Enif, at magnitude 2.38, is its brightest star; M15 is a bright globular cluster and NGC 7331 a spiral galaxy.
Per: Perseus belongs to the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the hero who killed Medusa and rescued Andromeda. An arc of stars along the Milky Way, Mirfak at its centre, between Cassiopeia and the Pleiades, marks it. It holds the Double Cluster (NGC 869 with NGC 884), visible to the eye, the open cluster M34 and the California Nebula (NGC 1499).
Phe: A constellation formed in the late 16th century, it is one of the 12 drawn from the observations of Dutch navigators in the southern seas. It shows the phoenix, the bird reborn from its ashes. Ankaa marks it, between Achernar and Fomalhaut; at magnitude 2.39, it is the brightest star of the constellation.
Pic: This is one of the 14 constellations created in the 18th century by a French astronomer after observing from the Cape of Good Hope; most are named after instruments of science and the arts. It shows the painter’s easel. It is a faint line of stars next to Canopus, toward the Large Cloud, and it holds β Pictoris, a young star with a disk of dust and planets.
PsA: Piscis Austrinus is among the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the southern fish, drinking the water poured by Aquarius. Fomalhaut, a lone bright star, marks it; the side of the Great Square of Pegasus from Scheat to Markab leads to it. Fomalhaut, at magnitude 1.16, is its brightest star.
Psc: Pisces is one of the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: two fish tied together by a cord, the form taken by Aphrodite and Eros to escape a monster. It is a V of faint stars around the Great Square of Pegasus, with a small ring of stars, the Circlet. Alpherg is its brightest star, and the face-on spiral galaxy M74 lies in it.
Pup: Puppis is the stern of the ship Argo of the Argonauts: part of a constellation of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century that was split into three in the 18th century. It lies on the Milky Way next to Sirius and Canis Major, toward Canopus. Naos, at magnitude 2.2, is its brightest star; M46, M47 and M93 are open clusters.
Pyx: A French astronomer created this constellation in the 18th century after observing from the Cape of Good Hope; it is one of 14 figures, most of them named after instruments of science and the arts. It shows the ship’s compass. It is probably a short faint line of stars between Puppis and the head of Hydra, with the planetary nebula NGC 2818 and T Pyxidis, a recurrent nova.
Ret: It belongs to the 14 constellations created in the 18th century by a French astronomer after his observations from the Cape of Good Hope, most of them named after instruments of science and the arts. It shows the reticle, the grid of a telescope eyepiece used to measure star positions. It is a small diamond of stars between Achernar and the Large Cloud.
Scl: This is one of the 14 constellations created in the 18th century by a French astronomer after observing from the Cape of Good Hope; most are named after instruments of science and the arts. It shows the sculptor’s workshop. It is a faint area between Fomalhaut and Achernar, with the Sculptor Galaxy (NGC 253), a bright spiral, and NGC 55, a spiral seen edge-on.
Sco: Scorpius belongs to the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the scorpion that killed Orion; the two are never in the sky together. A long curved line of stars with red Antares as its heart, beside Sagittarius, draws it; Antares, at magnitude 1.05, is its brightest star. M4 is a globular cluster near Antares, M7 a large open cluster visible to the eye and NGC 6231 a young open cluster.
Sct: It belongs to the 7 constellations that a Polish astronomer created at the end of the 17th century to fill gaps between older figures; all are still in use. It shows the shield, named in honour of a Polish king. A bright patch of the Milky Way, the Scutum Star Cloud, between Altair and the Teapot of Sagittarius, marks it. It holds M11, the Wild Duck Cluster, a rich open cluster, and the open cluster M26.
Ser: Serpens is among the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the serpent held by Ophiuchus, the only constellation split in two parts, head and tail. The head lies between Ophiuchus and the Northern Crown, the tail on the other side of Ophiuchus toward the Milky Way. It holds the bright globular cluster M5 and, in the tail, the Eagle Nebula (M16).
Sex: A modern constellation, created by a Polish astronomer at the end of the 17th century to fill gaps between older figures: it is one of the 7 still in use. It shows the sextant, an instrument for measuring the positions of stars. It is a very faint area next to Regulus and Alphard, with the Spindle Galaxy (NGC 3115), a lenticular galaxy seen edge-on.
Sge: Sagitta is one of the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the arrow, sometimes said to be the one shot by Heracles. A small arrow of four stars between Altair and Albireo, the head of the Swan, marks it. It holds the globular cluster M71.
Sgr: Sagittarius belongs to the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the archer, a centaur drawing his bow at the Scorpion. The Teapot asterism, beside the Scorpion’s tail, marks it; the centre of the Milky Way lies in that direction. Kaus Australis, at magnitude 1.79, is its brightest star; it holds the Lagoon Nebula (M8), the Trifid Nebula (M20) and the bright globular cluster M22.
Tau: Taurus is among the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the bull, the form taken by Zeus to carry off Europa. A V of stars, the Hyades, with Aldebaran, and the Pleiades nearby mark it: follow Orion’s belt away from Sirius. Aldebaran, at magnitude 0.87, is its brightest star; it holds the Pleiades (M45), the best-known open cluster, and the Crab Nebula (M1), the remnant of a supernova seen in 1054.
Tel: A French astronomer created this constellation in the 18th century after observing from the Cape of Good Hope; it is one of 14 figures, most of them named after instruments of science and the arts. It shows the telescope. It is a faint area next to the Teapot of Sagittarius and the small arc of Corona Australis.
TrA: This is one of the 12 constellations formed in the late 16th century from the observations of Dutch navigators in the southern seas. It shows the southern triangle. A bright triangle of three stars, Atria at one corner, next to the Pointers, marks it; Atria, at magnitude 1.91, is its brightest star. The open cluster NGC 6025 lies in it.
Tri: Triangulum is one of the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the triangle, sometimes seen as the delta of the Nile. It is a small narrow triangle of stars between Andromeda and Aries. The Triangulum Galaxy (M33), a face-on spiral of the Local Group, lies in it.
Tuc: It belongs to the 12 constellations formed in the late 16th century from the observations of Dutch navigators in the southern seas. It shows the toucan. Look for the Small Cloud, a pale patch visible to the eye near Achernar: it is a satellite galaxy of the Milky Way. Tucana also holds 47 Tucanae (NGC 104), one of the brightest globular clusters, and NGC 362.
UMa: Ursa Major belongs to the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the great bear, a nymph changed into a bear and placed in the sky. The seven stars of the Big Dipper form its back and tail, and the Pointers lead to the pole star. Alioth, at magnitude 1.76, is its brightest star; it holds M81, a bright spiral galaxy, M82, the Cigar Galaxy, and M101, the Pinwheel Galaxy, a face-on spiral.
UMi: Ursa Minor is among the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the little bear, whose tail ends at the pole star. Its Little Dipper runs from Polaris, at the end of the handle, to Kochab and Pherkad, the Guardians of the Pole. Polaris, at magnitude 1.97, is its brightest star.
Vel: Vela is the sails of the ship Argo of the Argonauts: part of a constellation of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century that was split into three in the 18th century. It lies on the Milky Way between Canopus and the Southern Cross, and shares the False Cross with Carina. It holds NGC 3132, the Eight-Burst Nebula, a planetary nebula, and IC 2391, an open cluster visible to the eye.
Vir: Virgo is one of the 48 constellations of the Greek catalogue of the 2nd century: the maiden holding an ear of wheat, linked to the goddess of the harvest or of justice. Spica marks it: continue the arc from the Big Dipper’s handle through Arcturus. Spica, at magnitude 0.98, is its brightest star; it holds M87, a giant elliptical galaxy with a jet at the heart of the Virgo Cluster, and M104, the Sombrero Galaxy.
Vol: A constellation formed in the late 16th century, it is one of the 12 drawn from the observations of Dutch navigators in the southern seas. It shows the flying fish. It is a small faint group between Carina and the Large Cloud, with the barred spiral galaxy NGC 2442.
Vul: It belongs to the 7 constellations that a Polish astronomer created at the end of the 17th century to fill gaps between older figures; all are still in use. It shows the little fox, first drawn with a goose in its jaws. It is a faint area between the Swan and the Arrow, inside the triangle of Vega, Deneb and Altair, with M27, the Dumbbell Nebula, a bright planetary nebula, and the Coathanger, an asterism visible in binoculars.
